_comment: Pre-market brief. Regenerated on a schedule and committed; the site only renders it. See tools/market-brief.md for how it is produced and what each field must contain. Everything here is written in our own words from sourced reporting — do not paste licensed article text into this file.
headline: Core PCE 3.0%. Bonds' worst month since 2022.
standfirst: Wednesday's data were all one way and the curve priced them at both ends. Core PCE rose 0.2% on the month and 3.0% on the year against 3.3% expected, after the BEA's annual update rewrote July down to 3.0%; ADP printed 90,000 against 70,000; final Q2 GDP was revised up to 2.2% from 1.5%; Chicago PMI jumped to 58.8 from 47.1. The front end took the inflation print and futures for 28 October fell to about 35–40% from about 50%; the long end took the growth prints and the ten-year and thirty-year rose again, closing a September in which the ten-year added about 50bp — its largest monthly rise since September 2022 and the worst month for Treasuries in four years. Stocks gave up a morning gain to end the quarter mixed, the S&P 500 down 0.25% to 7,651.54, the Dow down 0.86%, the Nasdaq up 0.24%; Micron beat and guided above consensus after the close. The November Brent contract expired at $103.53 and December, now the only price, is $96.95. Overnight the Nikkei rose 3.24% on the chipmakers, the Tankan held at 24, the yen fell to 158.3 on a cautious BoJ summary and China shut for Golden Week. Today: claims, ISM manufacturing, eight Fed speakers and Lagarde, Nike after the close. Tomorrow: payrolls.

bullets.title: PCE soft, GDP strong, ADP and Chicago hot: October slid to 35–40%
bullets.text: Core PCE rose 0.2% in August against 0.3% expected and 3.0% on the year against 3.3%, but the BEA's annual revision did most of the work, taking July down to 3.0% from 3.3% and headline July to 3.4% from 3.7%; August headline was +0.3% and 3.4%. Personal income rose only 0.2% against 0.4% while spending rose 0.9% against 0.8% and real spending 0.6% — households are funding the energy bill out of saving. Final Q2 GDP was revised up to 2.2% from 1.5% with the first quarter lifted to 2.5%: consumer spending 3.8%, business investment up 9%, imports up 12.6%, final sales to private domestic purchasers 4.6%, the price index 6.1%. ADP printed 90,000 against 70,000 with August cut to 36,000, job-stayers' pay up 3.2% and job-changers' 7.3%. Chicago PMI jumped to 58.8 from 47.1 against 51.2, its strongest since 2022. Futures for 28 October fell to about 35–40%; the Fed speakers did not follow — Kashkari said he still expects one more hike this year and another in 2027, Cook said inflation has been 'too high for too long', Goolsbee said inflation above target is 'playing with fire'. ECB October odds halved to about 30% during the week and the SNB's December odds fell to 31% from 71%.

bullets.title: Rates: a 50bp September on the ten-year, the thirty-year at a 2002 high, and a curve that keeps splitting
bullets.text: The ten-year rose about 50bp in September, its largest monthly rise since September 2022, and the thirty-year ended the month at its highest since 2002; Bloomberg's global aggregate index lost 2.4% in September, its worst quarter since the fourth quarter of 2024, and the Financial Times called the sell-off 'self-amplifying'. Wednesday repeated Tuesday's pattern: the three-month bill fell to 4.20% from 4.25% and the two-year to 4.88% on the soft PCE while the ten-year rose to 5.29% and the thirty-year to 5.64%, taking two-tens to 41bp from 37bp and bill-to-ten to 109bp, the widest of the cycle. Barclays still has the thirty-year at 6%. The long Treasury ETF fell 0.58% and is down 12.89% over twelve months; municipals rose 0.82%. In equities the S&P 500 fell 0.25% to 7,651.54 after rising on the PCE print, the Dow 0.86% to 50,906.05, the Nasdaq rose 0.24% to 26,861.06; Intel rose 3.7%, Apple 1.1%, Meta fell 1.84%. For September the Nasdaq gained 1.86% and the S&P 500 lost 0.45%, the Dow 4.29%; for the quarter the Nasdaq added 2.47%, the S&P 500 2.03% and the Dow lost 2.70%. Technology was the only sector up on the day, at +0.64%, and the only sector up on the month; staples fell 1.52%, health care 1.35%, industrials 1.27%. The VIX closed at 16.34. Europe: Stoxx 600 −0.4%, CAC −0.89%, FTSE −0.29%.

bullets.title: Micron: $54 billion of revenue, a $60–63 billion guide, and a stock that did not move
bullets.text: Micron reported fiscal fourth-quarter revenue of $54.23 billion, up 379% on the year and above the roughly $51.3 billion expected, adjusted earnings of $33.42 a share against about $31.70, a gross margin of 87% and fiscal-year revenue of $133.2 billion. It guided the current quarter to $60–63 billion in revenue and $37.15–39.15 a share against $57.4 billion and $35.47, said most of 2027's high-bandwidth memory supply is already contracted at higher prices, and raised capital spending again. The shares, up 273% this year, were little changed after hours — reports had them anywhere from 1.3% lower to 1.6% higher in the first hour — which is the tell: a beat of that size that does not move the stock says the beat was priced. Tokyo took it better: the Nikkei rose 3.24% towards 68,900 on Advantest, Tokyo Electron and SoftBank, and the Kospi gained about 1.6%; the Tankan held large manufacturers at 24 against 25 expected with the outlook up to 21 and capex plans +11.3%. Elsewhere the FTC is reported to be scrutinising OpenAI's and Anthropic's commercial arrangements, and Apple has set a smart-home event for 13 October, its first under John Ternus. Accenture reports before the open, seen $3.21 a share; Nike after the close, seen 45 cents, with prediction markets pricing a beat at about 69%.

bullets.title: Oil: the Brent roll is finished, exports are near pre-war, and refined products are the gap
bullets.text: The November Brent contract expired at $103.53, up 1%, and WTI settled at $90.42, up 1.2%; Brent gained about 14% in September and WTI 5%. This morning December Brent is $96.95, down 1.10%, and WTI $89.19, down 1.36% — the first session on which every front-month Brent chart shows the $6.50 gap, which no barrel traded through. Kpler counts at least 16.5 million barrels a day leaving the Gulf excluding Iran between 1 and 28 September, matching pre-war volumes via different routes, with Hormuz at 77%; Goldman has Gulf exports back to their 2025 average with about 5.2 million barrels a day in dark fleet, calls the market near balanced, and keeps Brent at $85 for year-end and $80 for 2027; JPMorgan says exports are at 98% of pre-war and that it does not know how to model the endgame. Refined product exports are at roughly half to 58% of pre-war, which is why heating oil is $4.64, diesel $6.53 a gallon at the pump, gasoline stocks at a 12-year low, and Trump is considering red-dyed diesel sales; the EIA reported crude stocks up 0.9 million barrels. On the diplomacy, Iran received the formal US response via Qatar — sequencing is the sticking point, with a seven-day trust-building plan toward an enhanced June memorandum — and Araghchi briefed the cabinet on Wednesday; Trump said 'you'll see things happening very soon' and denied offering sanctions relief; a tanker was attacked on Wednesday; the UK said there are 'strong indications' Iran was involved in the Fairford plot. Gold is $4,218.90, up 0.77%; the Bank of Korea said it will start buying gold in December.

bullets.title: Today and tomorrow: ISM, eight Fed speakers, Lagarde, Nike, Tokyo CPI, then payrolls
bullets.text: Thursday: Swiss CPI at 02:30 ET seen 1.0% after 0.8%, with the SNB's December odds down to 31%; euro-area unemployment at 05:00; Accenture before the open; claims at 08:30 seen 200,000 after 197,000; Barkin, Collins and Schmid on a panel at 09:05; Lagarde at 09:30 at the ESRB conference, the day after German inflation printed 3.3% against 3.1%, Italy 4.1%, France 3.4%, Spain 5.0%; final manufacturing PMI at 09:45 after a 57.0 flash; ISM manufacturing at 10:00 seen 55.0 after 54.6 with prices paid 72.3 after 71.1, and Waller at the same minute; Jefferson at 13:30, Bowman at 15:00, Cook and Williams at 15:30; Nike after the close; Tokyo CPI at 19:30 ET with core seen 2.4% after 1.8% as last year's energy subsidies drop out — the print that decides whether the BoJ's October is still live after the cautious summary of opinions. China is shut until 8 October. Friday: euro-area flash HICP at 05:00 ET seen 3.6% after 3.2% with core 2.5%, the print that decides whether 29 October is an ECB hike after this week's halving of the odds; payrolls at 08:30 with consensus 84,000–100,000 after 162,000, Barclays at 50,000, unemployment 4.1%, earnings +0.3%, after ADP's 90,000. Then Williams on 6 October, the FOMC minutes and ten-year auction on the 7th, the thirty-year, the ECB accounts and Musalem on the 8th, the banks on the 13th, CPI and the Beige Book on the 14th.

calendar.note: Seen 1.0% after 0.8%. The SNB's December hike odds fell to 31% from 71% this week; only a print above 1.0% puts them back.
Seen 200,000 after 197,000. The last labour print before payrolls, after ADP beat at 90,000 with August cut to 36,000.

calendar.event: Fed's Barkin, Collins and Schmid; Lagarde 09:30
calendar.note: Three regional presidents before ISM; Schmid votes this year. Lagarde speaks the day after German inflation printed 3.3% and the day before the euro-area flash, with October's ECB odds down to 30%.
Seen 55.0 after 54.6 with prices paid 72.3 after 71.1. Chicago said 58.8 and the flash PMI 57.0; a matching ISM keeps the long end's growth story alive on the day the front end prices a pause.

calendar.event: Fed's Jefferson; Bowman 15:00; Cook and Williams 15:30
calendar.note: The Vice Chair is the closest thing to the committee's centre that speaks. After a 3.0% core PCE and a 2.2% GDP the question is whether anyone still wants October.

calendar.event: Nike Q1 after the close; Tokyo CPI 19:30
calendar.note: Nike seen 45 cents, a beat priced at 69%. Tokyo core CPI seen 2.4% after 1.8%: the argument for a BoJ October move after the cautious summary and a yen at 158.
Seen 3.6% after 3.2%, core 2.5%, with Germany 3.3%, Italy 4.1% and Spain 5.0% already in. October's ECB odds halved this week; this print decides whether they come back.
Consensus 84,000–100,000 after 162,000, unemployment 4.1%, earnings +0.3%. October's Fed hike is priced near 35–40%; this is the print that sends it back to a coin flip or to December.

sessionNote: The first session of the fourth quarter opens with the curve split for a third day: the bill rate fell on a 3.0% core PCE, the ten-year rose on a 2.2% GDP and a 58.8 Chicago PMI, and both are consistent. The day has one data window — claims at 08:30 ET, ISM at 10:00 — and then eight Fed speakers spread from 09:05 to 15:30 ET, which means the afternoon tape is headline-driven and reverses easily. Stocks held the 7,650–7,690 gap again on Wednesday and closed at the bottom of it; Micron's non-reaction after a beat of that size is the day's cleanest read on positioning in semiconductors, and the Nikkei's 3.24% says Asia disagrees. Oil has one price again: December Brent near $97, WTI near $89. The yen at 158.3 has given back everything the joint US–Japan warning bought a week ago; Tokyo CPI at 19:30 ET is the next thing that can change that. With payrolls tomorrow and China shut all week, the session is positioning for Friday more than a view on Thursday.
watchOut: Treating the PCE print as disinflation. Core PCE at 3.0% against 3.3% expected reads like a three-tenth miss, but the BEA's annual update revised July to 3.0% from 3.3% and headline July to 3.4% from 3.7% — most of the gap is history rewritten, and August itself was merely soft at +0.2%. The front end traded it as a miss anyway, which is why October went to 35–40%; a hot ISM prices-paid at 10:00 ET or a firm payrolls tomorrow puts it back, and a reaction that reverses within the day is a reaction to positioning, not a change of view. The second trap is the Brent chart: every front-month continuation series gaps about $6.50 lower today because November expired at $103.53 and December is $97; no barrel traded through that gap, so it is not support, resistance or a sell-off. The third is quarter-start flow — the rebalancing that leaned on equities and the dollar into Wednesday's close unwinds in the first hour and looks like conviction. Size for a two-way 10:00 ET, keep the oil contract straight, and let the first hour's moves prove themselves.

archive.headline: October hike back to a coin flip.
archive.summary: Job openings fell to a five-month low, consumer confidence to a 2014 low and Williams said there was 'no need for urgency', taking October's hike from about 70% to about 50% priced; the two-year fell 6bp while the thirty-year touched 5.621%, its highest since 2002. Brent settled 2.6% lower on recovering Saudi exports, Australia's CPI printed 4.0% and the Aussie fell through 70 cents.

archive.headline: The ten-year closed at 5.24%. Nothing else mattered.
archive.summary: The ten-year closed at 5.236%, its highest since 2007, and the S&P 500 fell 0.77% to a ten-session low as Trump's rejection of Iran's Hormuz offer put Brent back above $107; Cook and Barkin talked rates higher, gold fell 3% to a seven-week low, and the RBA hiked to 4.60% overnight. The November Brent roll and Washington's reply to Tehran via Qatar were the day's traps.

archive.headline: Trump said no. Oil is back above $107.
archive.summary: Trump rejected Iran's seven-day Hormuz offer over the weekend and Brent recovered Friday's fall before New York opened; gold fell to its lowest since early August, the Kospi lost 2.5% and the dollar hit a two-month high. The front end eased with October's hike odds while the long end kept rising, into a week of PCE, ISM and payrolls.

archive.headline: The week the Treasury market stopped waiting for the Fed
archive.summary: Weekend edition. The ten-year went from 4.95% to 5.21% in a week on a 58.4 flash PMI, three auctions at two-decade highs and eight Fed speakers, and every Treasury from two years out cleared 5%. Equities held on Meta and AMD while the Dow fell for a fourth week, Brent round-tripped $100–$99–$106 on Iran, and October was 71% priced for a second hike.

archive.headline: A survey took the ten-year to 5.11%. An auction kept it there.
archive.summary: A flash composite PMI of 58.4, the highest since July 2021, took the ten-year up 14.6bp to 5.116% — its worst day since April 2025 — and a $70 billion five-year auction stopped at 5.033%, the highest since 2006. Barr said further hikes were likely needed and October went to 73% priced; every sector but energy fell and Brent rose back above $100.

archive.headline: The Fed said “we’ll see”. The two-year auction said 4.787%.
archive.summary: Treasury sold $69 billion of two-years at 4.787%, the highest stop since May 2024, on demand that held; Brent settled at $99.25 for its first close under $100 since 9 September; four Fed officials, none voting this year, all leaned toward more. The Nasdaq closed at a second straight record while financials fell 1.97%.

archive.headline: An App Store ranking moved a trillion dollars
archive.summary: Meta's Muse agent topped the US iPhone chart and the CPU complex repriced around it: Meta +11.43%, AMD +9.95% to a first $1 trillion close, Intel +12%, Arm +17%, and the Nasdaq to its first record since June. Crude fell to an eleven-day low on Hormuz shipping data and the ten-year came back under 5%, into a $69 billion two-year auction.
